parole.significato: rumen, paunch, fardingbag (first compartment of the stomach of a cow or other ruminants)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German wambe. Compare German Wamme and Wampe. First attested in 1398.
From Middle High German biutunge (“booty, allocation of spoils”), from Middle Low German bûte (“booty, plunder”) (compare German Beute). Possibly entered Hungarian via Czech bitung or bitunk.
Borrowed from Middle High German zil. Compare German Ziel.

parole.significato: false (not well-founded; not firm or trustworthy; erroneous)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German valsch.

parole.significato: weapon (an instrument of attack or defense in combat or hunting, e.g. most guns, missiles, or swords)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German fedeler (“trebuchet”). First attested in 1211.
First attested in 1367. Borrowed from Middle High German. Compare German Viertel.

parole.significato: prince (son or male-line grandson of a reigning monarch)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German herzog, from Old High German herizogo, from Proto-West Germanic *harjatogō.
Borrowed from Middle High German hamer (“hammer”).
From Middle High German hasart (“dice game”), from Arabic اَلزَّهْر (az-zahr, “the dice”).
From Middle High German holden (“to pay homage, swear fealty”), from hulde (“fealty, homage”) + -ol (verb-forming suffix).
From Middle High German katzer (“heretic”), from Medieval Latin Cathari (“the Pure”), name of a Christian sect, from Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós, “pure”).

parole.significato: cart, trap, barrow (a light two-wheeled vehicle used to carry a load and drawn or pushed by a person or animal)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Middle High German kordewagen.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From German Gucker, from Middle High German gücken, guggen (“to look inquisitively, peek, peer”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a specialised use of Middle High German gücken, gucken (“to cuckoo, call or cry like a cuckoo”), from Old High German guckōn, gukkōn (“to cuckoo”).

parole.significato: to roam, wander (to move or travel freely and with no specific destination)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German koberen (“to acquire; to gain strength”) + -ol (verb-forming suffix).
From Middle High German kosten, from Old High German kostōn (“to taste, attempt”) + -ol (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: a measure of volume for grain crop, lumpy material, or liquid (comprising 62, 94, or 125 liters, or 64–125 liters, or (…
parole.testo: From Middle High German kübel (“wooden vessel; this vessel as a measure of grain”), from Old High German miluhchubilī (“small milk can”), from Old Occitan cubel (“small vat”), from Latin cupa (“tub, cask, vat”). Compare German Kübel.
From Middle High German liberîe, from Old French livrée (“livery”), feminine past participle of livrer (“to deliver”), from Late Latin liberare (“to liberate”). With -éria ending.
First attested in 1405. From Middle High German planke, from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φᾰ́λᾰγξ (phắlănx).
From Middle High German part f (“share, part, party”), from Old French part, from Latin pars.

parole.significato: example (something serving to explain or illustrate a rule)
parole.testo: From Middle High German bilde (“picture, example, comparison”).
First attested in 1688. From Middle High German tartsche. Compare German Tartsche.

parole.significato: livestock merchant, cattle dealer (wealthy trader who bought livestock (especially cattle) in bulk to sell in major mar…
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German tewscher. Compare German Täuscher. First attested in 1419.

parole.significato: sentry, lookout, post (a strategically placed observation point where a watch is kept)
parole.testo: From Middle High German warte, compare German Warte.
Borrowed from Middle High German semele (“fine flour”), itself from Latin simila (“the finest flour”).
From the Middle High German salter (“psalm”), from the Medieval Latin psalterium (“psalter”), from the Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion, “a stringed instrument”).
From Middle High German sac, from Latin saccus (“sack”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sackcloth”), of Semitic origin.
From Middle High German schamel (“stool”); compare modern German Schemel.
A wanderword via either Middle High German anīs (“anise”) or Northern Italian. First attested in 1378.

parole.significato: cunning, insidious (of a person or group: scheming, seeking to harm or defraud others)
parole.testo: From Middle High German armman (“pauper”) + -os (occupational suffix). First attested in 1692.
